Isotopic labelling The symbol for the isotope introduced is placed in square brackets directly attached to the part of the name to which it refers (e.g. sodium ('4C]formate); appropriate arabic numerals and prefixes are added as necessary (e.g. L-[2-C]leucine). For simple molecules, chemical formulae may be used (e.g. 4#CO,). Square brackets should not be used when the isotopic symbol is attached to a word that is not a chemical name (e.g. “!*C-labelled”). Terms such as “'![-labelled albumin” should not be contracted to [3!T]albumin since native albumin does not contain iodine.

Genetics Genes and chromosomes The International Committee on Standardizing Human Gene No-menclature has developed a system knownas the International System. for Human Gene Nomenclature, but this is not universally accepted. Human genes are generally denoted by italicized symbols composed of capital letters, sometimes with the addition of an arabic numeral (e.g. CF, G6PD). Lower-case letters are commonly still used in blood-group symbols (e.g. Fy, Rh). Phenotype symbols are set in roman type (e.g. ADA 1).

Drugs and pesticides For pharmaceuticals the International Nonproprietary Names (INNs) should be used, and for pesticides the common names adopted by the International Organization for Standardization (see International Stan-dard ISO 1750:1981, and subsequent addenda and amendments). When no internationally approved name exists, an approved national name may be used. Proprietary names should be avoided whenever possible.

Oncogenes Oncogenes are usually designated by three-letter italic terms, often taken from the names of the viruses with which the genes are WHO Editorial Style Manual associated. A roman prefix may be added: “v-” for viral, “N-” for nuclear and “c-” for the gene’s cellular counterpart (proto-oncogene). Other prefixes and various suffixes are common. For example: Ha-ras-1 N-ras v-erb B yes c-abl fes/fps.

WHO Editorial Style Monval Interferons Interferons are represented by the symbol IFN to which is attached by a hyphen the Greek letter representing its type, for example IFN-a for alpha interferons. Non-allelic variants can be indicated by an arabic number or capital letter (sometimes subscripted) attached to the Greek letter. The prefixes “Hu” and “Mu” may be used to represent “human” and “murine” respectively. For example: MulFN-y HulFN-B — HulFN-c4. Interferon nomenclature. Journal of immunology, 1980, 125:2353.
Interferon nomenclature. Journal of general virology, 1984, 65:669-670.
